Shimla, 23 September 2026: The Tibet Advocacy Section of the Department of Information and International Relations (DIIR), Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), launched a Tibet Awareness Speaking Tour at Government College, Sanjauli, Shimla. The tour will continue at another college in Shimla on 24 September, after which the team will travel to Dalhousie on 25 September for talks at four Indian schools from 26 to 29 September.

The start of the tour coincides with the “Tibetan National Identity Preservation Week,” proposed by the Central Tibetan Administration to be observed during the fourth week of September every year. The opening talk was held in the spirit of the week, highlighting the urgency of preserving Tibet’s distinct identity, language, and culture.
Approximately 200 students and three faculty members attended the talk, which featured three speakers.

Tenzin Kunkhen of the Human Rights Desk, Tibet Advocacy Section, spoke on the current human rights situation inside Tibet under Chinese misrule. He highlighted the suppression of civil liberties and political freedoms, restrictions on religious practice, threats to Tibetan language education, the impact of colonial-style boarding schools and assimilationist policies on Tibetan children, and China’s so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Law. He also spoke about the self-immolation protests by Tibetans against Chinese repression inside Tibet, particularly that of Loga Rangzen.

Rinchen of the Tibet Advocacy Section, DIIR, spoke on “Why Tibet Matters” and Indo-Tibet relations. She emphasised the deep-rooted cultural, religious, and linguistic ties between Tibet and India, shaped by the spread of Buddhism and strengthened through centuries of pilgrimage and exile. She also underscored Tibet’s role as “Asia’s water tower,” vital to the water security of hundreds of millions of people in downstream regions, including India.

Dhondup Wangmo, Researcher at the Tibet Policy Institute, CTA, spoke on China’s environmental destruction and mining in Tibet. She outlined the threats posed by large-scale mining, hydropower dams, retreating glaciers, and increasing militarisation, and their consequences for traditional Tibetan livelihoods and for the countries that depend on rivers originating in Tibet.

The speakers encouraged students to learn more about Tibet, share accurate information, and raise their voices for an end to human rights violations and China’s occupation of Tibet. At the conclusion of the talk, the speakers donated a collection of books on Tibet to the college library.
The talk was held with the support of Prof. Bharti Bhagra, Principal, Government College, Sanjauli.
The talks at both colleges in Shimla have been organised with the help and coordination of the Chief Representative Office, Shimla, with the assistance of Ramjam, staff at the office.
_– Report filed by Tibet Advocacy Section, DIIR, CTA_
